title: The Cigar and the Steppe: an Argentine Duellist Who Ends as a General of the Tsar
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, birth in the barrio of San Nicolás
stops.date_confidence: year only, and traditional: the year comes from Pastor Obligado's 1903 chronicle by way of later dictionaries. No baptismal entry has been produced by any consulted source, and Cutolo's Nuevo diccionario biográfico argentino calls the man Benito rather than Benigno.
stops.campa: Benigno Benjamín Villanueva is born in the barrio of San Nicolás, in a Buenos Aires five years into revolution and already sorting itself into the factions that will fight for the next forty. His father is Miguel de Villanueva, said to have stood in the defence of the city against the English in 1807 and later to have marched with the Army of the Andes; his mother is Rafaela Lozada y Reyes. The parish books have never been made to yield the son. Everything that follows rests on a chronicle printed in Barcelona eighty eight years later.
sources: Pastor S. Obligado, Tradiciones Argentinas (Barcelona: Montaner y Simón, 1903)
suggested_refs: The parish registers of San Nicolás de Bari, Buenos Aires, never yet searched for this baptism

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the schools of Rufino Sánchez and Acosta
stops.date_confidence: no year is given in any source; 1825 is placed here only to hold the schooling in sequence between the birth and the duel.
stops.campa: The boy is sent to the schools of Rufino Sánchez and of Acosta, the ordinary classrooms of a porteño household with a soldier at the head of it. José de San Martín has crossed the Andes and gone into European exile; Martín Miguel de Güemes is dead in Salta. The wars the fathers fought are already being taught to the sons as history. No source dates a single year of this schooling. What the schoolroom supplies is a schoolmate, and in ten years Villanueva kills him.
suggested_refs: The private schools of Rufino Sánchez and of Acosta, Buenos Aires, 1820s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the cigar at the Café de los Catalanes
stops.date_confidence: month and year per the source (April 1835); the day is a default. Traditional throughout: no criminal record, no name for the dead man.
stops.campa: At the old Café de los Catalanes, beside the Iglesia de la Merced, Villanueva is at the billiard table when a quarrel over a cigar begins with a man the tradition makes a former schoolmate. They settle it with sabres and the schoolmate dies. Juan Manuel de Rosas has just taken the governorship back with the suma del poder público, and the city is a city of uniforms and denunciations. The opponent's name is nowhere written down. The month, the café, the church next door and the cigar are the whole of the record.
suggested_refs: The Café de los Catalanes and the Iglesia de la Merced, Buenos Aires, in the first year of Rosas's second governorship

stops.name: Buenos Aires Province, sentenced to the ranks
stops.date_confidence: year per the source; month and day are defaults set just after the April duel.
stops.campa: The sentence for the killing is service in the ranks: not a cell but a saddle, the standard disposal of an inconvenient young man in Rosas's Buenos Aires. Villanueva rides out to the province a common soldier, twenty years old, with no rank, no patron and a death behind him. María Remedios del Valle had served these same armies through the independence wars and been left begging in the streets of this same capital. The frontier takes him in. When the record produces him again, four years later, he is an officer.
suggested_refs: The practice of penal enlistment in the Buenos Aires provincial forces under Rosas

stops.name: Buenos Aires, lieutenant of the escort's second squadron
stops.date_confidence: year only, per the source, which gives the rank as held by 1839 without a promotion date.
stops.campa: By 1839 the common soldier is a lieutenant of cavalry commanding the second squadron of the government escort, the guard that rides at the governor's own person. Four years have carried him from a sabre killing in a billiard room to the inner ring of the Federal state. The source names no engagement and no order of promotion to explain the climb. Carlos María de Alvear's generation had made careers of this shape in the independence wars; Villanueva makes his in the civil ones, on the winning side of them.
suggested_refs: The escolta del gobierno of Buenos Aires province, the governor's mounted guard

stops.name: Tapalqué, the combat on the frontier line
stops.date_confidence: full date per the source; his presence is tradition, appearing in no muster roll.
stops.campa: The escort rides south to Tapalqué, on the line of forts that separates the estancias from the open pampa and the indigenous nations who still hold it. Frontier service in these years is raid and counter raid, cattle taken and cattle recovered, a war that produces few battles with names. Villanueva's presence at the combat of Tapalqué is one line in a chronicle. Thirty years on, Julio Argentino Roca will march past this same line of forts and take everything beyond it.
suggested_refs: The Tapalqué fort and the southern frontier line of Buenos Aires province, 1830s

stops.name: Chascomús, the rising broken at the laguna
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 7 November 1839; his presence is traditional. Drafts circulating with 'November 1847' for this battle are wrong by eight years.
stops.campa: On the shore of the laguna at Chascomús the free trade estancieros of the south rise against Rosas and are broken in an afternoon. Their leaders are shot within days and their heads set up in the plazas. Villanueva rides on the winning side, inside the machine. This is the one stretch of his Argentine career the later tellings pass over quickly: the man Buenos Aires will remember as an Argentine soldier abroad earns his first rank putting down Argentines at home.
sources: Standard chronology of the Libres del Sur rising, 1839
suggested_refs: The laguna of Chascomús and the defeat of the Libres del Sur, 7 November 1839

stops.name: Rodeo del Medio, the interior crushed
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 24 September 1841; his presence rests on the chronicle, with no muster roll quoted by any source.
stops.campa: At Rodeo del Medio, outside Mendoza, Villanueva serves under General Ángel Pacheco as the Unitarian coalition of the interior provinces is destroyed and Cuyo is closed to Rosas's enemies for a decade. The Andes stand at his back, the wall San Martín crossed with an army twenty four years before. This is the deepest inland point of his American service and the last battle any source places him in on Argentine soil. What comes next is water: the Paraná, the Uruguay, and the siege lines above Montevideo.
suggested_refs: The field of Rodeo del Medio, Mendoza, 24 September 1841

segments.name: The Littoral and the Long Siege

stops.name: Montevideo, into the lines of the siege
stops.date_confidence: 16 February 1843 is the attested opening of the siege; the date of Villanueva's arrival in the lines is not given anywhere.
stops.campa: Villanueva crosses to the Banda Oriental and joins the encirclement of Montevideo: Manuel Oribe's army in the hills, the city below fed by a French fleet and held by exiles and foreign legions. He serves under Nicolás Granada, Ángel Pacheco and Oribe, and then, at a date no source supplies, changes sides and serves inside the walls under General José María Paz. Anita Garibaldi is in that city in these years, with the Italian legion her husband commands on the defences Villanueva has been besieging.
suggested_refs: The Cerro and the Ciudadela of Montevideo during the Guerra Grande, 1843-1851

stops.name: Corrientes, on Paz's staff and the only words in his own voice
stops.date_confidence: year only, and traditional. The es.wikipedia article's Corrientes service is unsourced within the article; the quoted remark is dated to the 1844 campaign by inference from Obligado's narrative order.
stops.campa: On the Corrientes frontier Villanueva serves in the war of the littoral provinces against Rosas, among men who cross the Paraná to raid and cross back. The chronicle keeps one remark of his about the army of Madariaga he is sent to appraise, and it is the only sentence in the whole file that anyone claims is his. Pastor Obligado, printing it in Barcelona in 1903, calls the man who said it a young man of a very clear talent, and adds that he was right.
stops.quote: La instrucción de este ejército se parece á la de un hombre que hubiese aprendido aritmética sin saber leer ni escribir.
stops.quote_source: Pastor S. Obligado, 'Soldado argentino, general en Rusia,' Tradiciones Argentinas (Barcelona: Montaner y Simón, 1903), scan p. 152, reporting the remark as Villanueva's. Commonly and wrongly cited to José María Paz, Memorias póstumas.
suggested_refs: Obligado's Tradiciones Argentinas, pp. 152-153, the passage that carries both surviving Villanueva remarks

stops.name: Montevideo, the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: 8 October 1851 is the attested capitulation. Whether Villanueva was anywhere near it is the contradiction this stop exists to display.
stops.campa: The siege ends on the eighth of October 1851, eight years and nearly eight months after it closed, when Oribe capitulates and Urquiza turns west to finish Rosas at Caseros. The account that carries Villanueva keeps him in these lines for the whole encirclement. The same account has agents of Santa Anna hire him away to Mexico in 1846. Both statements stand in one file, five years of overlap between them, and no source has ever put a word in the gap.
sources: Standard chronology of the Guerra Grande
suggested_refs: The capitulation of Oribe's army before Montevideo, 8 October 1851

stops.name: Havana, under the guns of the Morro
stops.date_confidence: no source places Villanueva in Havana. This stop is the atlas's inference from the route between the Río de la Plata and Veracruz, and the date is a bare year holding it in sequence.
stops.campa: The road from the Río de la Plata to Veracruz runs through Havana, under the guns of the Morro, where every ship in the Gulf coals and every piece of news changes hands. Antonio López de Santa Anna has been in exile on this island and is negotiating his way home; his agents are hiring foreign officers wherever a hardened man can be found, and an Argentine cavalryman with a decade of civil war in him is exactly the article wanted. No passenger manifest naming Villanueva has been located in any port record.
sources: Atlas inference from the route; no source claim
suggested_refs: Havana as the coaling and news exchange of the Gulf, 1840s

stops.name: Veracruz, landing under San Juan de Ulúa
stops.date_confidence: the sources give only that agents of Santa Anna contracted him in 1846; the month is a default and the landing point is inferred from the fact that Veracruz was the port of entry.
stops.campa: He lands at Veracruz in the shadow of San Juan de Ulúa, in a country already losing a war it has hardly begun to fight. The United States holds the north; Santa Anna is assembling an army out of conscripts and whatever professionals will take his pay. Within a year this same port will fall to Winfield Scott's landing and become the base of the march inland. Villanueva enters Mexican service here, at the start of a campaign the sources compress into eight weeks and three battles.
suggested_refs: The fortress of San Juan de Ulúa and the port of Veracruz on the eve of Scott's landing

stops.name: La Angostura, the pass south of Saltillo
stops.date_confidence: the battle ran 22-23 February 1847, two days; the file carries the opening day. His presence is traditional, with no regiment and no arm of service named.
stops.campa: On the twenty second and twenty third of February, in the pass south of Saltillo the Americans call Buena Vista, Santa Anna throws an army worn thin by a desert march against Zachary Taylor's smaller force. The attack nearly succeeds and then does not; Santa Anna claims the victory and withdraws south in the night, leaving his wounded on the field. The chronicle places Villanueva in this battle without a regiment, without an arm of service, and without a roster to set him in any line of it.
sources: Standard chronology of the Battle of Buena Vista
suggested_refs: The narrows of La Angostura on the Saltillo road, fought 22-23 February 1847

stops.name: Hacienda del Sacramento, the crossing above Chihuahua
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 28 February 1847. His presence is traditional and the six days separating it from Angostura, some six hundred miles south, are not addressed by any source.
stops.campa: Six days later, at the crossing of the Sacramento river fifteen miles above Chihuahua, General José A. Heredia's force is broken by Alexander Doniphan's Missouri volunteers and the city is opened to occupation. Governor Ángel Trías had organised the defence; Pedro García Conde commanded the cavalry. The chronicle puts Villanueva here as well, six days and six hundred miles from the pass at Angostura, and offers no account whatever of how he crossed the distance.
sources: Standard chronology of the Battle of the Sacramento
suggested_refs: The Sacramento river crossing north of Chihuahua city, 28 February 1847

stops.name: Cerro Gordo, the National Road above Plan del Río
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 18 April 1847; his presence is traditional. Coordinates corrected from a drafted point 14 km west that effectively named Xalapa.
stops.campa: On the National Road above Plan del Río, in the pass at Cerro Gordo, Santa Anna fortifies the last position between Scott and the capital and has it turned by a flanking column cut through the scrub on his left. The army breaks and loses most of its guns. It is the third and last battle the sources credit to Villanueva's Mexican service: an itinerary of eight weeks that carries one man from Coahuila to Chihuahua to Veracruz across a country coming apart under him.
sources: Standard chronology of the Battle of Cerro Gordo
suggested_refs: The pass of Cerro Gordo on the camino nacional, turned 18 April 1847

stops.name: Mexico City, the flag over the Palacio Nacional
stops.date_confidence: attested: the capital capitulated on 14 September 1847. What Villanueva does afterwards is recorded nowhere at all.
stops.campa: The city capitulates on the fourteenth of September and the flag of the United States goes up over the Palacio Nacional. The cause Villanueva was hired to serve is finished, along with half the territory of the republic that hired him. What he does for the next year is not written down anywhere: no discharge, no passage, no letter, no witness. The next time a chronicle sets him on the ground he is in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, selling flour and shovels to men washing gravel.
suggested_refs: The occupation of the Palacio Nacional, Mexico City, September 1847

stops.name: Coloma, the tailrace at Sutter's Mill
stops.date_confidence: 24 January 1848 is the attested date of Marshall's find, not of Villanueva's arrival. His arrival is undated and cannot precede late 1848: the find was not public even in San Francisco until March 1848.
stops.campa: James Marshall picks metal out of the tailrace at Sutter's Mill in January 1848. The news reaches San Francisco in March, and Mexico and Chile before the year is out, and the first great wave into the diggings is Latin American: Sonorans, Chileans, Peruvians, working the placers by methods the Anglo arrivals of 1849 learn from them before driving them off the ground. Villanueva comes north into this country. He does not dig, and nothing in the record fixes the month he arrives.
suggested_refs: Sutter's Mill at Coloma and the Latin American placer camps of 1848-1849

stops.name: Sacramento Valley, the store instead of the claim
stops.date_confidence: year only and reconstructed. The source says Sacramento Valley, not the city, which was only laid out in 1849; a store 'in Sacramento' in 1848 is anachronistic.
stops.campa: In the Sacramento valley, where the supply road for the whole northern district runs, Villanueva opens a general store and sells to the miners rather than joining them. The town of Sacramento is laid out in 1849 at the junction of the two rivers and is a city inside a year. The tradition says he grows rich here, and this is the only stretch of his life in which he is reported making money instead of war. It is also the stretch with the least behind it: no licence, no partner, no address, no name over a door.
suggested_refs: The supply trade of the Sacramento Valley, 1849-1851

stops.name: San Francisco, out through Yerba Buena Cove
stops.date_confidence: year only, and inferred from the tradition's placement of him in Madrid by 1852-1853. No sailing, ship or route is named in any source.
stops.campa: He leaves through San Francisco, past the forest of hulls in Yerba Buena Cove abandoned by crews who ran for the diggings. From this waterfront the story reverses direction and never comes back: east by Panama or around the Horn, to Spain, to a war on the Black Sea, to a Russian regiment. Everything American in Villanueva's life ends here. The chronicle adds that he carried his California money to Madrid and lost it at the tables, which is the last thing it says about the money.
suggested_refs: The abandoned fleet in Yerba Buena Cove, San Francisco, 1850-1852

segments.name: Madrid, Prim, and the Eastern Question

stops.name: Madrid, the poet and the general
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources give the Madrid period loosely as 1852-1853 with no fixed month for the introduction.
stops.campa: In Madrid the California money goes at the tables and Villanueva is left holding introductions instead of capital. The poet Ventura de la Vega presents him to General Juan Prim y Prats, who will one day pull down a queen and carry Spain's crown around Europe looking for a taker. Spain is neutral in the quarrel gathering between Russia and the Ottomans and means to send officers to watch it fought. Prim is going as an observer, and Villanueva attaches himself to the mission.
sources: Isidoro Gilbert, El oro de Moscú (2011), at second hand
suggested_refs: Prim's Spanish observer mission to the Eastern war, 1853-1854

stops.name: Paris, the antechamber of every war
stops.date_confidence: the sources give Paris as a bare waypoint with no date, address or companion; the year is placed here to hold the sequence between Madrid and the Black Sea.
stops.campa: The road to the Eastern war runs through Paris, as every road in this century does. Mikhail Bakunin had conspired here through the 1840s before Russia had him brought back in irons; he is in a fortress of the Tsar at this moment, and will still be in one while Villanueva is collecting promotions in the Tsar's army. The sources give Paris and nothing else: no street, no companion, no date beyond a year inferred from the ones around it. The mission goes on east toward the Danube.
suggested_refs: Paris as the staging point of European military missions to the Eastern war

stops.name: Sinop, the harbour burned at anchor
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 30 November 1853 (18 November Old Style). Villanueva's presence at it is traditional and rests on the single Argentine chronicle; the two tags do not travel together.
stops.campa: At Sinop on the thirtieth of November, Admiral Nakhimov's squadron catches Osman Pasha's Ottoman fleet at anchor and destroys it with shell guns in a few hours, killing some three thousand men in the harbour. The European press calls it a massacre, and the calling of it that is what brings Britain and France into the war. The Argentine tradition puts Villanueva at the water's edge as a Spanish observer, watching the Russian navy do the thing that will shortly make Russia his employer.
sources: Standard chronology of the Battle of Sinop
es.wikipedia, 'Benigno Benjamín Villanueva' for his attendance
suggested_refs: The Russian shell-gun action in Sinop harbour, 30 November 1853

stops.name: Tutrakan, crossing to the Russian side on the Danube
stops.date_confidence: France declared war on Russia on 27 March 1854 and Britain on 28 March; drafts citing 28 March for both name only the British declaration. The identification of the sources' 'Totorkan' with Tutrakan on the Danube is this atlas's conjecture, not a source reading.
stops.campa: France declares war on Russia on the twenty seventh of March and Britain on the twenty eighth. Villanueva, whose own country is neutral and whose patron Prim serves the side now arming against Russia, crosses over and takes service with the enemy of his hosts. William Holman Hunt, painting at the Dead Sea this spring, writes that the war has just opened a thousand miles to the north of him. The chronicle sends Villanueva to the Danube towns it spells Totorkan, into the fighting around Silistra that opens the war.
sources: Standard chronology of the Anglo-French declarations, 27-28 March 1854
suggested_refs: The Danube campaign around Silistra, spring and summer 1854

stops.name: Sevastopol, written into the 31st cavalry division
stops.date_confidence: 17 October 1854 is the attested opening of the bombardment of Sevastopol; the date of Villanueva's incorporation is not given, and no source ties him to the siege lines by name.
stops.campa: He is written into the first regiment of the thirty first cavalry division, under a colonel the sources name variously Ponekkine, Ponnekin, Pouchkine and Pushkin. The tradition has him teaching Russian troopers to throw the lasso and the boleadoras of the pampa. Francisco de Miranda had ridden this same peninsula seventy years earlier as Potemkin's guest, granted the right to wear Russian uniform in any court of Europe; Ibn Battuta came ashore at Kaffa five centuries before that. For the Argentine no enrolment paper of any kind survives.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Benigno Benjamín Villanueva' (footnote 10 for the colonel's name variants)
suggested_refs: The Russian cavalry order of battle in the Crimea, 1854-1855

stops.name: Crimea, colonel in Ponekkine's place
stops.date_confidence: year only and traditional. The source says he succeeded Ponekkine as colonel of the regiment, not as commander of the division; no Russian record of the promotion has been produced.
stops.campa: Ponekkine is killed and Villanueva takes the regiment in his place, a colonel of Russian cavalry ten years after he was a lieutenant of Rosas's escort. Taras Shevchenko is serving out the Tsar's sentence in the Kazakh steppe in these same years, forbidden to write or to paint. The empire that raises the Argentine keeps the Ukrainian in a garrison at Novopetrovsk. Neither the promotion nor the man appears in any Russian officer roll that anyone has since been able to find.
sources: A. I. Sizonenko, Rodina 1995, nos. 3-4, p. 86, for the negative
suggested_refs: The Russian army officer rolls of the Crimean campaign, searched by Sizonenko with a negative result

stops.name: Sevastopol, the Malakoff and the burning of the fleet
stops.date_confidence: attested: the French took the Malakoff on 8 September 1855 and the city was evacuated that night. Villanueva's connection to the siege is not attested by any source.
stops.campa: On the eighth of September the French take the Malakoff, the Russians burn their fleet and cross the harbour bridge out of the city, and eleven months of siege end in rubble. Mark Twain will walk this ground twelve years later with the Quaker City party and be received by Alexander II at Livadia; a century and a half on, Vladimir Putin will fly Silvio Berlusconi over the same shoreline to look at the Greek stones at Chersonesus. The Argentine said to have held a regiment here has left no mark on it at all.
sources: Standard chronology of the fall of Sevastopol
suggested_refs: The Malakoff bastion and the evacuation of Sevastopol, 8-9 September 1855

stops.name: Paris, the treaty that ends the war
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Treaty of Paris was signed 30 March 1856. Villanueva is not a party to it and is not placed in the city; the stop marks the end of the war he changed flags for.
stops.campa: The Treaty of Paris is signed on the thirtieth of March: Russia gives up the mouths of the Danube and the right to keep a Black Sea fleet, and the war Villanueva changed flags for is finished. He is a colonel of a defeated army, not yet married into it, holding a rank no gazette records. The Spanish mission he came east with has long since gone home. Whatever he is now, he is it in Russian, and the next thing the chronicle does is change his name.
sources: Standard chronology of the Treaty of Paris, 1856
suggested_refs: The Congress and Treaty of Paris, 30 March 1856

stops.name: St Petersburg, the marriage and the change of name
stops.date_confidence: year only and traditional. The source names no city at all, only the court of the Tsar; St Petersburg is this atlas's placement, on the ground that the Spanish embassy sat there.
stops.campa: In 1857 Villanueva marries Ponekkine's widow, takes the surname Villanokoff and is made general. The chronicle gives him as padrino Luis Tomás Fernández de Córdoba y Ponce de León, Duke of Medinaceli, and calls him Spain's ambassador at the court of the Tsar. The duke was a senator and a knight of the Golden Fleece and held no diplomatic post in his life. Spain's ambassador extraordinary at St Petersburg from 1856 to 1868 was Mariano Téllez-Girón, Duke of Osuna, who is not mentioned.
sources: Standard biography of the 15th Duke of Medinaceli
Standard record of the Spanish embassy at St Petersburg, 1856-1868
suggested_refs: The Spanish embassy at St Petersburg under the Duke of Osuna, 1856-1868

stops.name: St Petersburg, decorated by Alexander II
stops.date_confidence: year only and traditional; the month is a default. No orders are named by the chronicle and no Russian award gazette carrying either Villanueva or Villanokoff has been produced.
stops.campa: Alexander II decorates him. The chronicle does not name the orders, and nobody since has produced a Russian gazette of awards carrying either Villanueva or Villanokoff. Pastor Obligado, who supplies all of this, is a Buenos Aires tradicionista writing half a century afterwards at the far end of an ocean from any Russian archive. These honours are the high point of the legend at home: the duellist out of the billiard room, decorated by the Tsar of All the Russias, with an Argentine name spelled the Russian way.
suggested_refs: Russian imperial award gazettes for 1856-1857, in which the name does not appear

stops.name: Moscow, the settled years
stops.date_confidence: no source fixes an address, a command or a date for this interval; the year is a placeholder for the sixteen years between the Crimean War and the Central Asian campaign.
stops.campa: Between the end of the war and the Central Asian campaigns lie sixteen years that the chronicle crosses in a clause. Villanokoff is placed in Moscow, married into the Russian officer class, a general with an adopted name and a Russian household. No address survives, no command, no assignment, no order of the day. The Almanaque Gotha is said to be printing his name on the army rolls through all of it, and that annual line will turn out to be the last thing anyone can point to and read.
sources: Obligado 1903, p. 148, for the Gotha rolls
suggested_refs: The Almanaque Gotha army lists for the 1860s and 1870s

stops.name: Orenburg, the column forms for Khiva
stops.date_confidence: Veryovkin's Orenburg column marched in late February 1873; the day is a default. The chronicle dates the campaign 1872, a year in which no Russian assault on Khiva took place, and Villanueva's presence is unattested in any case.
stops.campa: At Orenburg, the old staging base on the steppe from which Russia administers its Asian expansion, Veryovkin's column forms up in late February for the march on Khiva. Four columns are converging on the khanate: from Orenburg, from the Aral, from the Caucasus and from Turkestan, with Kaufman leaving Jizzakh in March. The chronicle puts Villanueva in this campaign and dates it to 1872, a year in which no Russian assault on Khiva takes place. It names no column and no command for him.
sources: Standard chronology of the Russian Khivan campaign of 1873
suggested_refs: The Orenburg column under Veryovkin, marching February 1873

stops.name: Khiva, the walls of the Ichan-Kala
stops.date_confidence: attested: Khiva fell 10 June 1873 and the khan was reinstated as a Russian client on 14 June. Villanueva's participation is traditional and undocumented.
stops.campa: Khiva falls on the tenth of June, the mud walls of the Ichan-Kala opened after a bombardment, the khan reinstated four days later as a client of the Tsar. It is the last of the great land seizures of Villanueva's lifetime and the last event any account fastens to him: Buenos Aires to the pampa forts, Montevideo to Veracruz, California to Madrid, the Danube to the Crimea, and now a walled oasis at the edge of the Kyzylkum. No roll of the four columns names him, and after this date no account places him anywhere at all.
sources: Standard chronology of the fall of Khiva, June 1873
suggested_refs: The Ichan-Kala of Khiva, taken 10 June 1873

stops.name: Russia, the death most of his biographers give
stops.date_confidence: year only, traditional, and contradicted twice over within the same account: by the Khiva campaign of 1873 and by the Gotha rolls running to 1875. No place of death is named; the Moscow pin is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Most of his biographers put the death here, in Russia, in 1872, with the rank of lieutenant general. The same accounts have him riding on Khiva the year after. No burial place is named, no widow's petition, no notice in a Russian paper, no stone anywhere. The life that opens with an unrecorded baptism in the barrio of San Nicolás closes with an unrecorded grave somewhere in the empire. The parish books at one end and the Russian registers at the other have produced nothing.
suggested_refs: Russian burial and army pension records, in which no Villanokoff has been found

stops.name: Russia, the name on the Gotha rolls to 1875
stops.date_confidence: year only; the claim is Obligado's and is offered by him against the 1872 death. The 1903 original reads 'el Almanaque Gotha', without the 'de' that later citations insert.
stops.campa: Obligado sets against the 1872 death one fact he says a reader could go and look up: that the Almanaque Gotha went on printing Villanueva's name in the ranks of the Russian army until 1875. He does not resolve the difference, and no one after him has. It is the only claim in the whole tradition that points at a document anybody could check, and what it is offered to prove is that the man was still alive three years after his own death. The volumes are on open shelves. Nobody has gone and looked.
stops.quote: hasta 1875 el Almanaque Gotha inscribía su nombre en el escalafón del ejército moscovita
stops.quote_source: Pastor S. Obligado, 'Soldado argentino, general en Rusia,' Tradiciones Argentinas (Barcelona: Montaner y Simón, 1903), scan p. 148. Later citations normalize the title to 'Almanaque de Gotha'; the 1903 text has no 'de'.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Obligado prints the tradition
stops.date_confidence: attested: the essay appears in Tradiciones Argentinas, Barcelona: Montaner y Simón, 1903, verified at Internet Archive item tradicionesargen00obliuoft. The book carries no month.
stops.campa: Pastor S. Obligado prints Soldado argentino, general en Rusia in his Tradiciones Argentinas, Barcelona, 1903. This is the source. Everything told about Villanueva for the next century, in newspapers, in books, in encyclopaedia articles, in this file, runs back to these four pages and to nothing else. Obligado praises the man's bearing, his easy manner and his astonishing facility in every language, and then, in the same sentence, notes that he could not write his own correctly.
stops.quote: en todas partes fue bien acogido por su caballerosidad, su afable trato, su inteligencia y amables maneras, la pasmosa facilidad para hablar todos los idiomas, aunque ni el propio escribía correctamente
stops.quote_source: Pastor S. Obligado, 'Soldado argentino, general en Rusia,' Tradiciones Argentinas (Barcelona: Montaner y Simón, 1903), scan p. 154. Quoted whole; the form in circulation stops at 'todos los idiomas' and drops the barb.
suggested_refs: Tradiciones Argentinas (Montaner y Simón, 1903), pp. 148-154

stops.name: Moscow, the descendants at the Revolution
stops.date_confidence: year only and traditional; no names, addresses or documents are attached to the claim in any source.
stops.campa: Direct descendants of Villanueva are said to be living in Moscow at the time of the Revolution, and that is the last of the family. No name is given for any of them, no street, no petition, no emigration record. After 1917 the line goes out as completely as the man did, in a city where a great many lines went out. Nothing further has ever been produced: no tomb, no monument, no portrait, no photograph, and not one line of writing in his own hand.
suggested_refs: Moscow residence registers of 1917, unsearched for this family

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Nación brings him back
stops.date_confidence: the date of the article is attested in the bibliography that carries it; the original newspaper page was not obtained, so the quotation is taken at second hand.
stops.campa: Estanislao F. Garay publishes Un argentino que fue general ruso in La Nación on the twenty sixth of March 1972, and the tradition comes back to a mass readership after seventy years of quiet. Garay explains the change of flags as chivalry: several nations against one, and Villanueva taking the weaker. The article that relays him adds, in its own footnote, that Prim had probably gone home to Spain by then, and that the resigned consent described here may never have been asked of anybody.
stops.quote: considerando que el enfrentamiento era desigual al batirse varias naciones contra una, toma partido, con la resignada anuencia de Prim, por el bando más débil, o sea el de los rusos
stops.quote_source: Estanislao F. Garay, 'Un argentino que fue general ruso,' La Nación, 26 March 1972, quoted in es.wikipedia, 'Benigno Benjamín Villanueva'. The newspaper page itself was not reached.
sources: La Nación, 26 March 1972, not reached: HathiTrust 403, Google Books API 429, web.archive.org blocked
suggested_refs: La Nación, 26 March 1972, the article that revived the legend

stops.name: Moscow, Sizonenko finds nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: Rodina, 1995, nos. 3-4, p. 86. The Russian issue was not obtained here and the finding is cited at second hand.
stops.campa: In 1995 the Russian historian Aleksandr I. Sizonenko publishes in Rodina an account of his search for Villanueva in the Russian military archives: the officer rolls, the award lists, the divisional records of the Crimean army. He finds nothing, and says so: no evidence that the man ever existed. Vicente Cutolo's Argentine biographical dictionary, meanwhile, calls him Benito. The archive and the reference works do not agree even on the man's given name.
sources: A. I. Sizonenko, Rodina, 1995, nos. 3-4, p. 86, cited at second hand
Cutolo, Nuevo diccionario biográfico argentino, cited via es.wikipedia footnote 3
suggested_refs: Rodina, 1995, nos. 3-4, p. 86, the archival negative

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the custodian calls it legend
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the book was not obtained here and the judgement is cited at second hand.
stops.campa: Isidoro Gilbert, whose El oro de Moscú carries the fullest Argentine telling of the story, judges it in the same book to be legend rather than history. That is where the file rests: the teller who preserves it does not believe it, and the archivist who went looking for it in Russia could not find a line. The atlas keeps the route all the same, San Nicolás to Khiva, because the route is what the canon says, and sets the rest down plainly beside it.
sources: Isidoro Gilbert, El oro de Moscú (2011), cited at second hand via es.wikipedia
suggested_refs: Isidoro Gilbert, El oro de Moscú (Buenos Aires, 2011), the fullest modern telling and its own disclaimer
